title: The fourth truth
hook: the way that leads to the ending of dukkha: the eightfold path

segments.voice: Yesterday: to be realized, and your line, taste it. Did you find one small taste of ease? Today, the last of the four truths: how to get there. Day three hundred forty-two.

Imagine a doctor who gives you a perfect diagnosis, explains exactly what's causing it, tells you with real confidence that it can be cured, and then stands up and leaves the room. No prescription. No plan. You'd be left holding three pieces of good information and nothing to do on Monday morning. The first three truths are the diagnosis, the cause and the hope. The fourth is what keeps the Buddha in the room. It's the most practical part of the teaching. Today, the fourth noble truth.
screen: `A PERFECT DIAGNOSIS.` → `THE DOCTOR LEAVES.` → `NOTHING TO DO ON MONDAY.`

segments.voice: The fourth truth is the way leading to the ending of dukkha. The Pali word is magga: a path, a road, a track through the forest. In the first sermon the Buddha names it: the noble eightfold path. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. The word translated right is sammā, which also means complete, whole, fitting, the way a well-made thing is right. Two things are worth noticing. First, this path is the middle way. The sermon begins by setting aside two extremes: chasing sense pleasure, and punishing the body. The eightfold path runs between them. Second, it's not eight steps in a row, like a staircase where you finish step one before starting step two. Teachers often compare it to the strands of a rope, or the spokes of a wheel, all working at once. Your speech affects your mindfulness; your mindfulness affects your view. You don't graduate from right speech. And look at how ordinary most of it is. Speech, action, the way you earn a living. Half the path happens at the kitchen table and at work, not on a cushion. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's 1881 translation, puts the fourth truth at the top of its list of bests: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." Over the next weeks of year two, we'll walk these eight one at a time. Today, just the map.
screen: `MAGGA: A ROAD THROUGH THE FOREST.` · `EIGHT FACTORS, NAMED.` · `STRANDS OF A ROPE, NOT STAIRS.` · `HALF AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.` · then, large: `THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to name the eight factors. Sit, and count them on your fingers, one per breath, slowly. View. Intention. Speech. Action. Livelihood. Effort. Mindfulness. Concentration. Then go around again, and this time, with each one, let a single picture from your own life come up: a conversation, a job, a moment of attention. If you forget one, don't worry. Just start the count again. The bell holds the time.
Magga. The path: the fourth noble truth, the noble eightfold path that leads to the ending of dukkha.
Your line: the path. Today, pick one of the eight that already shows up in your life, speech, effort, livelihood, and notice it once in action. Day three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhists of every school learn the noble eightfold path as the practical core of the teaching, and in many temples and homes the eight-spoked wheel stands for it.

myth: the eight factors are steps you finish one at a time
teachers compare them to strands of a rope or spokes of a wheel, all working together.
the eightfold path is the middle way between two extremes
the first sermon sets aside sense-pleasure and self-punishment, and names the path between.
the eightfold path is only about meditation
speech, action and livelihood are on it too: much of it happens at work and at home.

fork.setup: you've just heard the first three truths: dukkha, its cause, its ending. what's the one thing still missing?
options: a list of who's to blame.
a promise of reward after death.
fork.reveal: the fourth truth is the way: the noble eightfold path, which keeps the teaching from being diagnosis without treatment.

original.note: Pali magga, Sanskrit mārga: a path or road; the fourth noble truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: right means obeying rules correctly.
what it means: sammā means complete, whole, fitting; eight factors developed together.
what a scholar hears: the full name is dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, the practice leading to the cessation of dukkha, and SN 45.8 defines each of the eight factors in turn.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the fourth noble truth and the middle way
SN 45.8 (Vibhanga Sutta), the eight factors defined

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.quoted: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words

notes: Confirm exact Müller 1881 wording of Dhammapada 273 ('The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; ...').
The rope/wheel comparison for the simultaneity of the factors is a modern teaching image, not a sutta quotation; it is presented as what teachers say.
Sammā glossed as complete/whole/fitting: confirm with PED.
